docs.title: Experimental Validation of Control Methods
docs.text:
Welcome to the supplementary website accompanying my research internship thesis: Data-driven Optimal Control on Quanser Qube.

Author: Jort Stammen Supervisors: Sasha Pogromskiy (TU/e), Dragan Nesic (UoM), Mathieu Granzotto (UoM) Institutions: Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) & The University of Melbourne

docs.title: About This Website
docs.text:
This website presents videos and additional results from the experimental evaluation of data-driven and model-based control methods on physical hardware. Because the dynamic behavior of the closed-loop systems—such as disturbance rejection, recovery, and servo drift—cannot be fully captured on paper, this platform provides a visual complement to the results presented in the thesis.

Figure: The Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 experimental setup used for all validations.

docs.title: The Experiments
docs.text: The videos are categorized according to the structure of the thesis. Each section demonstrates the real-world application of Discounted Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR) on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 rotary inverted pendulum.

docs.title: Data-Driven Methods (Chapter 3 & 5)
docs.text:
Experiments investigating direct and indirect data-driven controller designs from measured input-state data, without prior system identification.

  • Inertia Disc: Servo angle tracking and reference following.
  • Pendulum Balance Control: Stabilizing the pendulum using probing data, demonstrating robustness against programmed pulse disturbances.
  • Noisy Data Designs: Demonstrating the conservatism and robustness of relaxed LMI designs under measurement noise.

Explore Data-Driven Experiments

docs.title: Model-Based Methods (Chapter 2 & 5)
docs.text:
Experiments investigating model-based controller design and its experimental performance using known system dynamics.

  • Guaranteed Cost & Gain Error: Demonstrating convex LMI-based designs (\({\hat{K}_\gamma}\) and \({\bar{K}_\gamma}\)).
  • Stabilizing Policy Iteration (sPI): Iterative approaches to finding stabilizing near-optimal gains.
  • Robustness & Sweeps: Multi-push disturbance tests and sweeps over the decay rate (\(\alpha\)) and discount factor (\(\gamma\)) to observe hardware limitations like servo drift and voltage saturation.

Explore Model-Based Experiments

docs.title: How to Use This Website
docs.text: Select an experiment from the navigation menu to find: 1. Objective: What the specific experiment aims to prove. 2. Setup: The controller parameters used (e.g., \(\gamma\), \(\alpha\), \(T_s\)). 3. Videos: High-framerate recordings of the physical tests. 4. Observations: Key takeaways, such as settling time, peak deviations, and steady-state behavior.

docs.title: Relation to the Thesis
docs.text: All experiments shown here correspond directly to Chapter 5 (Experimental Results) of the thesis. The theoretical groundwork for the controllers can be found in Chapter 2 (Model-based) and Chapter 3 (Data-driven), while the hardware specifics are detailed in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Model-Based Controller Experiments
docs.text:
This section presents the experimental validation of the model-based control methods investigated during the research internship.

Because the optimal discounted LQR controller is often unstable on the actual hardware (for discount factors like \(\gamma = 0.5\)), we designed and tested alternative state-feedback controllers. These controllers enforce a guaranteed decay rate (\(\alpha\)) using Linear Matrix Inequalities (LMIs) while remaining as close to optimal as possible.

The experiments follow a chronological progression, moving from initial baseline tests to detailed parameter sweeps to find the physical limits of the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2.

docs.title: 1. Baseline Controllers
docs.text:
The first experiments conducted on the hardware test the three primary controller designs at a nominal setting (\(\alpha = 0.98, \gamma = 0.5\)). These tests evaluate disturbance rejection and steady-state behavior. A key observation from these baseline tests is that while the pendulum is stabilized, the guaranteed gain error design experiences severe servo drift, prompting further investigation.

👉 View Baseline Controller Experiments

docs.title: 2. Decay Rate (\(\alpha\)) Sweep
docs.text:
Following the baseline experiments, a crucial question arose: Is the servo drift a fundamental flaw of the controller, or just a result of the chosen decay rate \(\alpha\)?

This set of experiments sweeps the decay rate \(\alpha\) from 0.99 down to 0.94 to find the practical operating window. We observe three distinct regimes on the hardware: 1. Large \(\alpha\) (\(\ge 0.98\)): Pendulum is stable, but the servo wanders (drift). 2. Intermediate \(\alpha\) (\(\approx 0.965 - 0.975\)): The "sweet spot" where both the pendulum and servo converge nicely. 3. Small \(\alpha\) (\(\le 0.96\)): The controller becomes too aggressive, hitting the actuator voltage saturation limit (\(\pm 10\) V) and causing limit-cycle oscillations.

👉 View \(\alpha\)-Sweep Experiments

docs.title: 3. Discount Factor (\(\gamma\)) Sweep
docs.text:
Once the optimal decay rate window was identified (\(\alpha = 0.97\)), a final set of experiments was conducted to test the effect of the discount factor \(\gamma\).

These experiments vary \(\gamma\) between 0.2 and 0.9 to answer how the loop's behavior changes depending on how heavily we discount the future. We observe that the guaranteed-cost design (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\)) is highly sensitive to \(\gamma\) and saturates at high values, while the guaranteed-gain error design (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\)) remains largely independent of \(\gamma\) due to active constraints.

👉 View \(\gamma\)-Sweep Experiments

docs.title: Model-Based Baseline Controllers
docs.text: Before performing extensive parameter sweeps, the three proposed model-based control strategies were implemented and tested on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 using a nominal set of baseline parameters.

docs.title: Baseline Parameters
docs.text:
Unless otherwise specified, the controllers in this section were synthesized using the following parameters:

  • Sample Time (\(T_s\)): 10 ms
  • Discount Factor (\(\gamma\)): 0.5
  • Guaranteed Decay Rate (\(\alpha\)): 0.98
  • State Cost (\(Q\)): \(\text{diag}(100, 30, 10, 1)\)
  • Input Cost (\(R\)): 10

Below, you can explore the videos, theoretical guarantees, and experimental observations for each specific controller.

docs.title: Guaranteed Cost Design (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
This approach synthesizes a gain by solving a convex optimization problem that minimizes an upper bound on the cost of the closed-loop system, ensuring the system decays at the prescribed rate \(\alpha\).

  • Observation: Successfully balances the pendulum and keeps the servo relatively stationary without hitting actuator saturation limits.

View the Guaranteed Cost Controller Experiment

docs.title: Guaranteed Gain Error Design (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
Instead of bounding the cost directly, this design aims to find a stabilizing gain that is as close as possible (in the spectral norm sense) to the optimal—but unstable—discounted gain \(K^\star_\gamma\).

  • Observation: While it successfully balances the pendulum, the hardware tests reveal significant servo drift/wandering at this specific \(\alpha\) value, highlighting a limitation that is explored further in the \(\alpha\)-sweep.

View the Guaranteed Gain Error Controller Experiment

docs.title: Stabilizing Policy Iteration (sPI)
docs.text:
The sPI algorithm is an iterative approach (a variant of policy iteration) that improves a stabilizing gain step-by-step. It uses a convex combination of the previous gain and the standard policy improvement step to ensure every iteration remains stabilizing with respect to \(\alpha\).

  • Observation: Shows monotonic theoretical cost improvement, though the final stability margin ends up resting exactly on the boundary of the allowed decay rate \(\alpha\).

View the sPI Controller Experiments

docs.title: Guaranteed Cost Controller (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
The guaranteed cost design synthesizes a gain by minimizing an upper bound on the cost of the closed-loop system, while enforcing a strict decay rate of \(\alpha = 0.98\) (with \(\gamma = 0.5\)).

In the hardware tests, this controller successfully balances the pendulum (\(\delta\phi\) converges to zero) and keeps the servo arm relatively stationary, recovering well from manual disturbances.

docs.text:

docs.title: Guaranteed Gain Error Controller (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
The guaranteed gain error design aims to find a stabilizing gain that is as close as possible to the optimal (but unstable) discounted gain \(K^\star_\gamma\). We use a baseline decay rate of \(\alpha = 0.98\).

While this controller successfully balances the pendulum, the hardware tests reveal an interesting limitation: the servo arm experiences severe servo drift (wandering). This drift occurs because the controller prioritizes mimicking the optimal gain over stiffening the servo loop, a phenomenon we investigate deeply in the \(\alpha\)-sweep.

docs.title: Experimental Validation vs. MATLAB Simulation
docs.text:
The videos below show the physical hardware response alongside the real-time servo angle (\(\psi\)) plotted in MATLAB, clearly illustrating the drift.

MATLAB: Servo Angle Physical Experiment ⏯ Play / Pause 🔄 Restart

docs.title: Stabilizing Policy Iteration (sPI)
docs.text:
The sPI algorithm is an iterative approach that improves a stabilizing gain step-by-step. By taking a convex combination of a standard policy improvement step and the previous gain, it ensures that every iteration remains stabilizing with a prescribed decay rate (\(\alpha = 0.98\)).

The performance of the final sPI controller heavily depends on its initialization (\(K_0\)).

docs.title: 1. Initialized with Guaranteed Cost (\(K_0 = \hat{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
When initialized with the guaranteed cost gain, the algorithm converges monotonically. Below, the physical behavior is compared with the balance error (\(\delta\phi\)).

MATLAB: Balance Error Physical Experiment ⏯ Play / Pause 🔄 Restart

docs.title: 2. Initialized with Guaranteed Gain Error (\(K_0 = \bar{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
When initialized with the guaranteed gain error, the resulting controller exhibits the characteristic servo drift seen in its parent controller. Below, the physical behavior is compared with the servo angle (\(\psi\)).
